newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. envoy flies to meet Zairean rebel leader.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy flies to meet Zairean rebel leader.

text.p: A U.N. envoy was due in Zaire's northeastern city of Kisingani on Saturday to press rebel leader Laurent Kabila for a ceasefire following the return of Zaire's ailing president.
Diplomats said Mohamed Sahnoun, joint envoy of the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity, was believed to be carrying a special message and proposals for a ceasefire.

He left Nairobi by plane for Kisangani a day after a low-key homecoming by President Mobutu Sese Seko to Kinshasa which contrasted with a hero's welcome for Kabila on his arrival in Zaire's northeastern capital seized by the rebels a week ago.

"We are made to understand that he (Sahnoun) is carrying a special message for Kabila," a diplomat told Reuters. "We are also made to understand he is going to present new proposals on a possibility for a ceasefire in Zaire."

A political source told Reuters that Kabila was coming under heavy pressure to call a ceasefire, particularly after Mobutu said he no longer ruled out talks with the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL).
"He now risks being labelled 'the bad boy' if he continues to refuse to do so," the source said. Kabila has so far insisted on negotiations with Mobutu, or his representative, before any ceasefire.
"We negotiate first," said Kabila, rejecting the president's call for a truce followed by talks as he arrived on Friday in Kisangani, where he was welcomed by more than 10,000 jubilant residents.
The AFDL has seized more than a fifth of Zaire, Africa's third largest country, since October and put to flight the notoriously ill-disciplined Zairean army and its foreign mercenaries.
Diplomats said Sahnoun, who discussed the Zaire crisis on Friday with Ugandan president and regional power broker Yoweri Museveni, would probably fly to Kinshasa after talks with Kabila.

Kabila's rebel force is dominated by ethnic Tutsis, some of them Zairean Banyamulenge Tutsis and others said by intelligence sources to be members of Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army. The Rwandan government denies any involvement with the rebels.
Demobilised Ugandan troops, hired on contract, are also part of the rebel force. Kabila is a Zairean non-Tutsi from Shaba and his field commanders are a mixture of Zaireans and foreigners.
With Mobutu's popularity in Kinshasa plummeting, the United States said on Friday it was sending hundreds of troops to West Africa to prepare for a possible evacuation of Americans from Zaire.
They would join French troops and planes already in nearby Gabon and Congo in case evacuations from Zaire became necessary.
Exhausted by fresh cancer treatment and a difficult flight home from France, Mobutu, 66, sent away a senior welcoming committee and the world's press at Kinshasa airport on Friday.
"It was a difficult flight," one close aide told Reuters, adding that Mobutu was resting at his official residence.

Mobutu, 66, has spent most of his time in Europe since prostate cancer surgery in August. He has dominated Zaire with a mixture of political acumen and military ruthlessness since seizing power in 1965.

He left hospital in Monaco on Wednesday after treatment and issued a statement on Thursday calling for a truce and for a national council to find ways out of the crisis "with all our brothers, without exclusion".

Many ordinary Zaireans, eager for a change from poverty and hardship under Mobutu, are openly rallying to Kabila, who has said the central diamond capital of Mbuji-Mayi and Zaire's second city Lubumbashi in the southeast are next in his sights.
